subject: science
title: US Middle School Science — Human Body Systems Reading
subtitle: Reading passages on body systems, evidence, and homeostasis
description: A source-faithful middle school life science pack on how major human body systems work and interact. It covers digestion, breathing, circulation, nervous system responses, homeostasis, data interpretation, and Claim-Evidence-Reasoning explanations.

data.sourcePassage: The human body is a system made of smaller interacting systems. No single system can keep the body alive by itself. The digestive system breaks food into nutrients such as glucose and amino acids. The respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. The circulatory system carries oxygen and nutrients to cells and carries wastes away. The nervous system detects information, sends signals, and helps coordinate movement, breathing, heart rate, and responses. During exercise, these systems become easier to notice because muscles need more oxygen and glucose and produce more carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which system breaks food into nutrients?
questions.modelAnswer: The digestive system breaks food into nutrients.

questions.question: Which system transports oxygen and nutrients to cells?
questions.modelAnswer: The circulatory system transports oxygen and nutrients to cells.

questions.question: Why are body systems better described as interacting rather than separate?
questions.modelAnswer: They depend on each other for materials, signals, and responses, such as oxygen from the lungs being carried by blood to cells.

questions.question: Explain why exercise makes body system interactions easier to observe.
questions.modelAnswer: Exercise increases muscle demand for oxygen and glucose and increases carbon dioxide production, so breathing and heart rate usually rise.

questions.question: How could a student use evidence to show that systems interact during exercise?
questions.modelAnswer: A student could compare pulse and breathing rate before and after exercise and explain that increases show transport and gas exchange responding to muscle needs.

data.sourcePassage: Digestion changes food into molecules small enough for the body to absorb and use. Mechanical digestion physically breaks food apart, such as when teeth chew food or the stomach churns. Chemical digestion uses enzymes and acids to break large molecules into smaller molecules. Most nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine. Tiny finger-like villi increase the surface area so more nutrients can move into the blood. The large intestine mainly absorbs water and helps form solid waste. Food does not turn directly into energy. Instead, food contains molecules with stored chemical energy, and cells release usable energy from glucose during cellular respiration.

questions.question: Where does most nutrient absorption occur?
questions.modelAnswer: Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine.

questions.question: Which example is mechanical digestion?
questions.modelAnswer: Teeth chewing food is mechanical digestion.

questions.question: Why do villi help the small intestine absorb nutrients?
questions.modelAnswer: Villi increase surface area, which allows more nutrients to move into the blood efficiently.

questions.question: Correct this misconception: food turns directly into energy.
questions.modelAnswer: Food contains molecules with stored chemical energy. Digestion breaks food into molecules, and cells use glucose and oxygen during cellular respiration to release energy.

questions.question: How do the digestive and circulatory systems work together after a meal?
questions.modelAnswer: The digestive system breaks food down and absorbs nutrients, and the circulatory system carries those nutrients in blood to body cells.

data.sourcePassage: Air enters the nose or mouth, travels through the trachea, moves into the bronchi, and reaches tiny alveoli in the lungs. Alveoli are suited for gas exchange because they are numerous, have thin walls, have moist surfaces, and are surrounded by capillaries. Oxygen moves from the air in alveoli into the blood. Carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the alveoli and leaves the body when a person exhales. The heart pumps blood through two main loops. Pulmonary circulation moves blood between the heart and lungs. Systemic circulation moves blood between the heart and the rest of the body.

questions.question: What are alveoli?
questions.modelAnswer: Alveoli are tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange occurs.

questions.question: Which gas moves from alveoli into the blood?
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen moves from alveoli into the blood.

questions.question: Why do thin alveoli and capillary walls help gas exchange?
questions.modelAnswer: Thin walls create a short distance for oxygen and carbon dioxide to move between air and blood.

questions.question: What is the difference between pulmonary and systemic circulation?
questions.modelAnswer: Pulmonary circulation moves blood between heart and lungs, while systemic circulation moves blood between heart and the rest of the body.

questions.question: Why is it inaccurate to say that the heart gives blood oxygen?
questions.modelAnswer: The heart pumps blood, but oxygen enters blood at the lungs, especially across alveoli and capillaries.

data.sourceTitle: Nervous System Responses and Reaction Time
data.targetTitle: Nervous System Responses and Reaction Time
data.sourcePassage: The nervous system detects information, sends signals, and coordinates responses. A stimulus is a change that can cause a response. In a stimulus-response pathway, sensory neurons carry information toward the brain or spinal cord. The information is processed, and motor neurons send signals to muscles or glands. In a ruler-drop reaction test, the eyes detect the ruler moving, the brain processes the information, and hand muscles contract to catch the ruler. Distractions, tiredness, hand used, practice trials, and time of day could affect results. A fair test changes only one variable at a time and uses repeated trials.

questions.question: What is a stimulus?
questions.modelAnswer: A stimulus is a change that can cause a response.

questions.question: In a ruler-drop test, which body part detects the ruler moving?
questions.modelAnswer: The eyes detect the ruler moving.

questions.question: Why should a reaction-time investigation use repeated trials?
questions.modelAnswer: Repeated trials make the data more reliable and reduce the effect of mistakes or unusual results.

questions.question: How could background noise affect reaction time?
questions.modelAnswer: Background noise could distract the student, making it take longer to notice the stimulus or respond.

questions.question: Identify the independent and dependent variables in a test of noise and reaction time.
questions.modelAnswer: The independent variable is the noise condition, and the dependent variable is reaction time or ruler catch distance.

data.sourcePassage: Homeostasis means keeping internal body conditions within a healthy range even when conditions change. It does not mean that the body stays exactly the same all the time. Heart rate, breathing rate, body temperature, water level, blood sugar, oxygen, and carbon dioxide all need regulation. During exercise, muscle cells use more oxygen and glucose and produce more carbon dioxide and heat. Breathing rate usually increases to bring in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide. Heart rate usually increases to move blood faster. Sweating can help cool the body. These changes help the body return toward stable conditions.

questions.question: What does homeostasis mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Homeostasis means keeping internal body conditions within a healthy range.

questions.question: Which example shows homeostasis?
questions.modelAnswer: Sweating when hot is an example of homeostasis.

questions.question: Why does breathing rate usually increase during exercise?
questions.modelAnswer: Muscle cells need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide, so faster breathing helps exchange gases.

questions.question: Why is homeostasis not the same as staying exactly unchanged?
questions.modelAnswer: The body changes heart rate, breathing, sweating, and other responses to keep conditions within healthy ranges.

questions.question: Use Claim-Evidence-Reasoning to explain how activity affects pulse rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Claim: activity increases pulse rate. Evidence: measured pulse rises after exercise. Reasoning: muscles need more materials and produce wastes, so faster blood flow helps transport them.
